pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Associative property of addition — when adding three or more numbers, they may be grouped (added) in any order without changing the total, e.g. (2+3)+5 = 2+(3+5). For ages 6–7, layered on commutativity and used as a strategy tool, not a stated law.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 pupils 'show that addition of two numbers can be done in any order (commutative) and subtraction of one number from another cannot'; associative grouping underpins Y2 'add numbers using... a three-digit number and ones/tens' and the Y3 formal written methods where partial sums are recombined. Named explicitly as a mental strategy in KS2 guidance.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.3 'Apply properties of operations as strategies to add and subtract... To add 2+6+4, the second two numbers can be added to make a ten, so 2+6+4 = 2+10 = 12 (Associative property of addition).' Children need not use formal terms.
• Operational details: teach as a licence to regroup for convenience — look-for-a-ten, add doubles first, add the friendly pair. Contrast with commutativity (reorder) — association is about which pair you combine FIRST. Keep the whole conserved: the three quantities are unchanged, only the sequence of combining differs.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (age 6) — given 2+8+5, child chooses to add 2+8 to make 10 first and explains why that is allowed. Tier B (age 7) — regroups three addends two different ways and confirms the same total. Tier C (age 7+) — uses grouping to justify a mental strategy in a worded context and states that regrouping never changes the sum.
bestPractices: Introduce through the practical goal of making calculation easier (look for a pair that makes ten, or add a double first) rather than as an abstract named law.
Use concrete equal-status objects (counters, cubes) the child physically pushes into different pairs, so the conserved whole is seen while the grouping order varies.
Contrast explicitly with commutativity: reordering (which comes first) versus associating (which pair we combine first) — pupils confuse the two.
Have children compute the same triple by two different groupings and compare totals, making the invariance an observed result, not a told fact.
Connect forward to written column addition, where partial sums (ones, tens) are grouped and recombined, so the property is seen as load-bearing later.
keyRepresentations: Three counter groups / cube towers that can be pushed into different pairs before merging
Bracket notation over three addends, (a+b)+c vs a+(b+c), with the first-combined pair highlighted
Ten-frame showing a make-ten pair filling first, then the remainder added
Bar/part-whole model with three parts and one conserved whole bar
Empty number line where the child chooses which jump to take first
commonMisconceptions: Believing the total changes if you add in a different grouping (failing to conserve the whole).
Conflating associativity with commutativity — thinking they are the same 'any order' rule.
Losing track of an addend when regrouping (dropping or double-counting the third number).
Thinking brackets are just decoration rather than an instruction about what to combine first.

learn.summary: Teaches the associative property of addition for ages 6–7: when adding three or more numbers, any two can be combined first without changing the total, e.g. (2+8)+5 = 2+(8+5) = 15. The point is the freedom to choose which pair to combine first, used as a practical strategy (make a ten, add a double first) rather than as a stated law. Contrast with commutativity (reordering the numbers) and avoid over-generalising to subtraction, where (10−3)−2 = 5 but 10−(3−2) = 9. Includes hands-on manipulation, a reasoning/justification layer, consolidation checks, and a static side-by-side anchor, each with its pedagogical purpose and limits noted.

activities.title: Grouping bench: choose which pair to combine first
feedback: If a learner reaches the same total both ways, name the move: 'You grouped these two first — that's allowed, and the total stayed the same.'
If a learner expects the total to change under a different grouping, have them compute both groupings of the same triple side by side and compare the equal totals; stress the amounts are unchanged.
If a learner loses or double-counts the third addend after making a ten, physically set the third object aside and bring it in last, then recount — this is a tracking slip, not a concept error.
When a make-ten pair is chosen, point out how the second step (e.g. 10+5) became easy.
activities.rationale: The concept is the freedom to decide which pair to combine first, so letting the learner physically make and compare that choice is intended to turn invariance into an observed result rather than a told fact, and to surface WHY grouping helps. Standards frame this as a strategy, not a named law.
sourceClaims: 1.OA.3 applies properties of operations as strategies, giving the associative example 2+6+4 = 2+10 = 12 and noting children need not use formal terms.
Making ten by regrouping addends is a key mental calculation strategy in early KS1/KS2.
Y2 pupils show addition can be done in any order and use this alongside grouping when adding a three-digit number and ones/tens; formal written methods recombine partial sums.
learnerActions: Set out three equal-status objects or number tiles for a triple such as 2, 8, 5 (counters, cubes, or draggable tiles).
Choose any two to combine first; merge them into a single running sum, then bring in the third.
Try the same triple a second way (e.g. combine 8+5 first) and compare the final total.
State out loud which pair you combined first and why that choice made the calculation easier.
Repeat with a triple that rewards a make-ten pair (e.g. 2+8+5, where 2+8=10 then 10+5=15) and one that rewards adding a double first (e.g. 4+4+7, where 4+4=8 then 8+7=15).
activities.intendedInsight: You may choose which pair to combine first; a smart choice (make a ten, or add a double) makes the sum easier while the total stays identical because the three amounts themselves never change.

activities.title: Why is that allowed? Justify your grouping
feedback: If the learner justifies by pointing to the unchanged amounts, name that reasoning back as 'grouping'.
If the learner cannot say why the total is the same, return to combining the same triple two ways and comparing before asking again.
Probe with 'what's your evidence the total is still the same if you group differently?' to move from a one-off trick toward a general reason.

If a learner tries the subtraction pair, confirm (10−3)−2 = 5 but 10−(3−2) = 9 — the answers differ, so subtraction cannot be regrouped the way addition can; use this only as a contrast, never as a rule to apply.
activities.rationale: Early standards ask pupils to show/apply the property and explain their strategy, so an explain/justify layer is intended to develop the reasoning the numeric answer alone does not reveal; the subtraction contrast targets the common over-generalisation.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils show addition can be done in any order and use this alongside grouping when adding a three-digit number and ones/tens; formal written methods recombine partial sums.
1.OA.3 applies properties of operations as strategies, giving the associative example 2+6+4 = 2+10 = 12 and noting children need not use formal terms.
learnerActions: Given a triple, say which two numbers you would add first.
Answer a questioner (a peer, tutor, or 'maths buddy') who asks 'Why is that allowed?' and 'Would we get the same total if we grouped the numbers differently? How do you know?'
Explain in your own words that the three amounts are unchanged, so only which pair you combine first differs.

Try a new triple such as 4+7+6 and justify which pair you would add first (here 4+6=10, then 10+7=17). Notice that 4 and 6 are not next to each other, so adding them first means changing the order as well as the grouping; the total is still 17.
Test the contrast with subtraction: work out (10−3)−2 = 5 and 10−(3−2) = 9, notice the answers differ, and conclude that the grouping freedom belongs to addition, not subtraction.
activities.intendedInsight: Grouping is a reasoning move you can justify: the total is conserved because the three quantities stay the same, no matter which pair you combine first — but this freedom holds for addition, not for subtraction.

activities.title: Consolidate: match, choose, and check equal totals
feedback: For the efficient-pair item, confirm the make-ten pair and show the easy second step.
For a true/false item where a number was altered, point out that the total changed because an amount changed, not because of regrouping.
activities.rationale: Closed-response items are intended to consolidate recognition of equivalent groupings after hands-on work; whether they do so is not established here. This is a check/consolidation step; it does not by itself let a learner freely explore their own alternative groupings, and recognition alone does not elicit the learner's own production of a grouping.
learnerActions: Decide which pair you would add first to make a given triple easy (e.g. for 2+8+5, which pair makes a ten?).
Judge true/false statements about whether two groupings of the same triple share a total, including an item where one number has been changed so the total genuinely differs.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising equivalent groupings and spotting the efficient first pair is intended to consolidate that regrouping preserves the total while making the calculation easier.

activities.title: Side-by-side anchor: did the total change?
feedback: Confirm that the brackets changed which pair came first but the final total stayed the same.
If a learner treats brackets as decoration, point to the highlighted first pair and the matching final totals.
activities.rationale: A fixed side-by-side display is a clear reference anchor for the bracket-reading idea. It is a scaffold: because the triples are pre-set, it cannot let the learner test their own choice of grouping, which is the heart of the property.
learnerActions: Look at two pre-set groupings of the same triple, e.g. (2+8)+5 and 2+(8+5), with brackets marking each first pair.
Reveal each intermediate sum and the shared final total (both land on 15).
Answer 'Did the total change?' and explain what the brackets tell you to combine first.
activities.intendedInsight: Brackets are an instruction about what to combine first, not decoration, and both groupings reach the same total.

constraints: Teach as a licence to regroup for convenience (look for a ten, add a double first), not as an abstract named law; children need not use the formal term 'associative'.

Distinguish associativity (which pair we combine FIRST) from commutativity (which order numbers come in); learners frequently conflate them, so address them explicitly. Note that combining two numbers that are not next to each other first (e.g. 4 and 6 in 4+7+6, or 2 and 5 in 2+8+5) uses both properties together.
Do NOT extend the grouping rule to subtraction: (10−3)−2 = 5 does not equal 10−(3−2) = 9. Use this contrast to probe, not as a rule to apply.
Keep the whole conserved: the three quantities stay the same; only which pair is combined first differs. Guard against dropping or double-counting an addend during regrouping.

Closed matching/true-false items and the fixed side-by-side anchor are consolidation and reference scaffolds; they do not let a learner freely explore alternative groupings and should follow, not replace, hands-on choice. This is an observable limit of those formats, not a claim that only manipulation can teach the concept.

The optional interactive touches (a total bar pinned at a fixed value while intermediate sums recompute, a make-ten pair glowing, tiles fusing on drag) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit arithmetic: 2+8+5=15 and 2+6+4=12 are correct in both groupings; 4+4+7=15; 4+7+6=17. The deliberately altered true/false distractor should change a number so the total genuinely differs — do not present two correct groupings as giving different totals.
Subtraction check: (10−3)−2 = 5 and 10−(3−2) = 9, so subtraction is NOT associative; this is used only as a contrast/probe in the justify activity, never taught as working.
Source note: the CCSS-M claim and the NCETM claim are marked verified:false in the row; the DfE claim is marked verified:true. Confidence should not be upgraded on that basis.

Activity 2's sourceClaims evidence associativity as a strategy and the 'show' of the property; they do not directly evidence the justify/explain pedagogy or the subtraction contrast, which rest on the pedagogy's misconception list rather than a cited claim.

The original 3D-interactive entry was judged a poor fit with the boilerplate reasoning 'a flat concept is not made 3D by rendering it in 3D'; this universal-sounding claim is not established by the source material and was dropped rather than propagated as a law.
The forward connection to column addition (recombining partial sums) is carried only in standards framing, not as its own activity; a follow-on activity could make that link explicit.

assess.poeTask: Predict whether adding (2 + 8) first or (8 + 5) first changes the answer to 2 + 8 + 5. Say your prediction and why. Then work out both ways and check — what does the result tell you about grouping?
probeDeeper: Why did you choose those two numbers to add first?
What's your evidence the total is still 15 if you group the numbers differently?
What if the numbers were 4 + 7 + 6 — which pair would you add first, and why?
Does this grouping trick work for subtraction? Try (10 − 3) − 2 and 10 − (3 − 2) and see.
assess.correctAnswer: 15. A strong answer adds 2 + 8 to make 10 first, then 10 + 5 = 15, choosing that pair because it makes a ten. The total is 15 whatever grouping is used — the three amounts don't change, only which pair is combined first.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'You have to add them in the order they're written' — adds strictly left-to-right and resists regrouping to make a ten.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build (2+8)+5 and 2+(8+5) with cubes side by side; both reach 15. Establish that you may choose any pair to combine first.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Insists on 2+8 then +5 only because that is the written order; will not try 8+5 or 2+... to make ten.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks a different grouping changes the total.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compute two groupings of the same triple side by side and compare the equal totals; stress the amounts are unchanged.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — grouping them differently would give a different total.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts a different answer if the numbers are grouped another way.

errorPatterns.pattern: Loses or double-counts the third addend after making a ten.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the concept — physically set the third tile aside and bring it in last; check the count.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Makes ten with two numbers then forgets to add the third, or adds it twice.

responseLevels.gap: Adds left-to-right only, cannot regroup, or believes a different grouping changes the total.
responseLevels.full: Explains the total is conserved under any grouping because the three amounts are unchanged, and deliberately chooses a make-ten pair to make the calculation easier.
responseLevels.partial: Can add the three and may even use make-ten, but cannot explain why any grouping gives the same total, or treats it as a one-off trick for this case.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work out 2 + 8 + 5. Which two numbers did you add first, and why did you pick those? Would you get a different total if you added them in a different order?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child adding mechanically left-to-right can still reach 15, so the numeric answer alone doesn't discriminate. The 'which did you add first / would a different order change it' tier reveals whether the child sees grouping as a free, total-preserving choice (and spots the make-ten pair) or believes the written order is fixed / that regrouping changes the total.
